english: Finally there also arises the problem whether, for every given algebraic branching configuration with a prescribed branching scheme, an associated algebraic configuration actually exists.
topic: Defines a first and second genus (p_1, p_2) of a space by the number of cut surfaces needed so that every closed surface, respectively every closed curve, can be contracted to a point, raises the existence problem for algebraic configurations with a prescribed branching scheme (a generalisation of Riemann's existence theorem), and lists coloured relations between three functions U, V, W.

triage.modern_statement: Here is how I read the note. Take a complex algebraic variety X of dimension 2 or more, for example the projective plane or projective space. Take an algebraic subvariety B in it, the 'branching configuration'. Prescribe a 'branching scheme', meaning a finite topological covering of X minus B, which amounts to a transitive permutation representation of π1(X∖B), the fundamental group of X with B removed. The question is whether there is always an algebraic variety Y with a finite morphism Y→X, branched only over B, whose unbranched part is exactly that topological covering. This is the higher-dimensional version of Riemann's existence theorem for curves. The modern answer is that every finite topological cover of a normal complex algebraic variety minus a subvariety extends uniquely to a normal analytic branched cover, and that cover is algebraic.
triage.answered_by: H. Grauert and R. Remmert (1958), with the Grauert–Remmert extension theorem for analytic branched coverings (building on Stein). A. Grothendieck later gave an algebraic-geometric version in SGA 1 (1960–61), Exposé XII, Theorem 5.1: finite étale covers of X correspond exactly to finite topological covers of the underlying complex space X^an. This version uses Hironaka's resolution of singularities. Earlier, Enriques and others had studied special cases of covers of the plane.

evidence.claim: A survey on comparison theorems has a section on Riemann's existence theorem in higher dimension. It says the problem was settled by Grauert and Remmert, and afterwards by Grothendieck using Hironaka's resolution of singularities.

Wikipedia states the generalisation (Grauert–Remmert): the category of finite topological coverings of a complex algebraic variety is equivalent to the category of finite étale coverings of that variety.
SGA 1, Theorem XII.5.1 is cited as giving an equivalence between étale coverings of X and finite topological coverings of X^an.
The Grauert–Remmert extension theorem is used to complete topological coverings of a complement into branched coverings.
By the Grauert–Remmert–Stein theorem, a branched covering is uniquely determined by its unramified part.

triage.why: Hilbert's question asks whether an algebraic configuration exists for every given branching locus and prescribed branching scheme. That is exactly the existence half of Riemann's existence theorem carried to higher dimensions. The sources say this was settled by Grauert–Remmert (1958) and by Grothendieck in SGA 1, and it is now a standard tool. The fundamental groups of complements of branch curves are still studied, which is how one finds which schemes can occur, but the existence question itself is closed. I did not find any source that links this diary note directly to Hilbert's published problems. Confidence is medium because the note is short, and I am inferring that 'Verzweigungsgebilde/Verzweigungsschema' means 'branch locus plus monodromy'.
